But before one ventures on such conjectures, the Kerı̂ אי [where?] must be tried. Is it the abbreviated אין (Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Real-Wörterbuch</hi>, xiv. 712)? Certainly not, because וּלרוזנים אין שׁכר would mean: and the princes, or rulers (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding רוזנים at <reference osisRef="Prov.8.15">Pro 8:15</reference>), have no mead, which is inconsistent. But אין does not abbreviate itself into אי, but into אי. Not אי, but אי, is in Heb., as well as in Ethiop., the word with which negative adjectives such as אי נקי, not innocent, <reference osisRef="Job.22.30">Job 22:30</reference>, and in later Heb. also, negative sentences, such as אי אפשׁר: it is not possible, are formed.<note placement="foot">The author of the <hi type="italic">Comm</hi>. עטרת זקנים to the ארח חיים, c. 6, Geiger and others would read אי, because אי is abbreviated from אין. But why not from אין, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.9">1Sa 21:9</reference>? The traditional expression is אי; and Elias Levita in the <hi type="italic">Tishbi</hi>, as also Baer in the Siddur <hi type="italic">Abodath Jisrael</hi>, are right in defending it against that innovation.</note> <div eID="gen12006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12007" type="x-p"/> Therefore Mühlau vocalizes אי, and thinks that the author used this word for אל, so as not to repeat this word for the third time. But how is that possible? אי שׁכר signifies either: not mead, or: there is not mead; and both afford, for the passage before us, no meaning. Is, then, the Kerı̂ אי truly so unsuitable? Indeed, to explain: how came intoxicating drink to rulers! is inadmissible, since אי always means only <hi type="italic">ubi</hi> (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.9">Gen 4:9</reference>); not, like the Ethiop. aitê, also <hi type="italic">quomodo</hi>. But the question <hi type="italic">ubi temetum</hi>, as a question of desire, fits the connection, whether the sentence means: <hi type="italic">non decet principibus dicere</hi> (Ahron b. Josef supplies שׁיאמרו) <hi type="italic">ubi temetum</hi>, or: <hi type="italic">absit a principibus quaerere ubi temetum</hi> (Fleischer), which, from our view of 4a, we prefer. There is in reality nothing to be supplied; but as 4a says that the drinking of wine ought not to characterize kings, so 4b, that “Where is mead?” (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, this eager inquiry after mead) ought not to characterize rulers.<note placement="foot">The translation of Jerome, <hi type="italic">quia nullum secretum est ubi regnat ebrietas</hi> (as if the words were לית רזא אי שׁכר), corresponds to the proverb: נכנס יין יצא סוד :b, when the wine goes in the secret comes out; or, which is the same thing: if one adds יין (= 70), סוד (= 70) comes out.</note> <div eID="gen12007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12008" type="x-p"/> Why not? <reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">Pro 31:5</reference> says. That the prince, being a slave to drink, may not forget the מחקּק, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, that which has been made and has become חק, thus that which is lawfully right, and may not alter the righteous cause of the miserable, who cry against their oppressors, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, may not handle falsely the facts of the case, and give judgment contrary to them. שׁנּה דין (Aquila, Theodotion, Quinta, ἀλλοιοῦν κρίσιν) is elsewhere equivalent to הטּה משׁפּט (עוּת). בּני־עני are those who are, as it were, born to oppression and suffering. This mode of expression is a Semitism (Fleischer), but it here heightens the impression of the Arab. colouring. In כל (<hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ὡντινοῦν) it is indicated that, not merely with reference to individual poor men, but in general to the whole class of the poorer people, suffering humanity, sympathy and a regard for truth on the part of a prince given to sensuality are easily thrown aside. Wine is better suited for those who are in a condition to be timeously helped over which, is a refreshment to them.
entries.a3d9b218435be7a168323a00135c6f074be8a196: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.6-Prov.7.6">Pro 31:6-7 6</reference> Give strong drink to him that is perishing,    And wine to those whose soul is in bitter woe; 7 Let him drink and forget his poverty,    And let him think of his misery no more. <div eID="gen12008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12009" type="x-p"/> The preparation of a potion for malefactors who were condemned to death was, on the ground of these words of the proverb, cared for by noble women in Jerusalem (נשׁים יקרות שׁבירושׁלים), <hi type="italic">Sanhedrin</hi> 43a; Jesus rejected it, because He wished, without becoming insensible to His sorrow, to pass away from the earthly life freely and in full consciousness, Mar 15:23. The transition from the plur. to the sing. of the subject is in <reference osisRef="Prov.31.7">Pro 31:7</reference> less violent than in <reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">Pro 31:5</reference>, since in <reference osisRef="Prov.31.6">Pro 31:6</reference> singular and plur. already interchange. We write תּנוּ־שׁכר with the counter-tone <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> and <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>. אובד designates, as at <reference osisRef="Job.29.13">Job 29:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.19">Job 31:19</reference>, one who goes to meet destruction: it combines the present signification <hi type="italic">interiens</hi>, the fut. signif. <hi type="italic">interiturus</hi>, and the perf. <hi type="italic">perditus</hi> (hopelessly lost). מרי נפשׁ (those whose minds are filled with sorrow) is also supported from the Book of Job; <reference osisRef="Job.3.20">Job 3:20</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.21.25">Pro 21:25</reference>, the language and thought and mode of writing of which notably rests on the Proverbs of Agur and Lemuel (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Mühlau, pp. 64-66). The <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. τοῖς πικροῖς (not ψυξροῖς) τὴν ψυχήν. רישׁ (poverty) is not, however, found there, but only in the Book of Proverbs, in which this word-stem is more at home than elsewhere. Wine rejoices the heart of man, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.15">Psa 104:15</reference>, and at the same time raises it for the time above oppression and want, and out of anxious sorrow, wherefore it is soonest granted to them, and in sympathizing love ought to be presented to them by whom this its beneficent influence is to be wished for. The ruined man forgets his poverty, the deeply perplexed his burden of sorrow; the king, on the contrary, is in danger from this cause of forgetting what the law required at his hands, viz., in relation to those who need help, to whom especially his duty as a ruler refers.
entries.d3183241c54359ac0adddeec1375253b8c293269: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.8-Prov.9.8">Pro 31:8-9 8</reference> Open thy mouth for the dumb,    For the right of all the children of leaving; 9 Open thy mouth, judge righteously,    And do right to the poor and needy. <div eID="gen12009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12010" type="x-p"/> He is called dumb who suffers the infirmity of dumbness, as עוּר and פּסּח, <reference osisRef="Job.29.15">Job 29:15</reference>, is he who suffers the infirmity of blindness or lameness, not here figuratively; at the same time, he who, on account of his youth, or on account of his ignorance, or from fear, cannot speak before the tribunal for himself (Fleischer). With ל the <hi type="italic">dat. commodi</hi> (lxx after Lagarde, μογιλάλῳ; Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, ἀλάλῳ; the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. after Gebhardt, βωβῷ) אל, of the object aimed at, interchanges, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, 1Ki 19:3; 2Ki 7:7, אל־נפשׁם, for the preservation of their life, or for the sake of their life, for it is seldom that it introduces the object so purely as here. And that an infin. such as חלוף should stand as a subst. occurs proportionally seldomer in Heb. (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.4">Isa 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.7">Psa 22:7</reference>; cf. with ה of the artic., Num 4:12; <reference osisRef="Ps.66.9">Psa 66:9</reference>) than it does in Arab. בּני חלוף in the same way as בּני־עני, 5b, belongs to the Arab. complexion of this proverb, but without its being necessary to refer to the Arab. in order to fix the meaning of these two words. Hitzig explains after khalf, to come after, which further means “to have the disadvantage,” in which Zöckler follows him; but this verb in Arab. does not mean ὑστερεῖν (ὑστερεῖσθαι), we must explain “sons of him that remains behind,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, such as come not forward, but remain behind ('an) others. Mühlau goes further, and explains, with Schultens and Vaihinger: those destitute of defence, after (Arab.) khalafahu he is ranked next to him, and has become his representative - a use of the word foreign to the Heb. Still less is the rendering of Gesenius justified, “children of inheritance” = children left behind, after khallafa, to leave behind; and Luther, “for the cause of all who are left behind,” by the phrase (Arab.) khallfany'an 'awnih, he has placed me behind his help, denied it to me, for the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of the verb cannot mean to abandon, to leave. And that בני חלוף means the opposers of the truth, or of the poor, or the litigious person, the quarrelsome, is perfectly inadmissible, since the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> חלוף cannot be equivalent to (Arab.) khilaf, the inf. of the 3rd conj., and besides, the gen. after דּין always denotes those in whose favour, not those against whom it is passed; the latter is also valid against Ralbag’s “sons of change,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, who say things different from what they think; and Ahron b. Josef’s “sons of changing,” viz., the truth into lies. We must abide by the meaning of the Heb. חלף, “to follow after, to change places, pass away.” Accordingly, Fleischer understands by חלוף, the going away, the dying, viz., of parents, and translates: <hi type="italic">eorum qui parentibus orbati sunt</hi>. In another way Rashi reaches the same sense: orphans deprived of their helper. But the connection בני חלף requires that we make those who are intended themselves the subject of חלוף. Rightly Ewald, Bertheau, Kamphausen, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.2.18">Isa 2:18</reference> (and Psa 90:5., this with questionable right), and understand by the sons of disappearance those whose inherited lot, whose proper fate, is to disappear, to die, to perish (Symmachus: πάντων υἱῶν ἀποιχομένων; Jerome: <hi type="italic">omnium filiorum qui pertranseunt</hi>). It is not men in general as children of frailty that are meant (Kimchi, Meîri, Immanuel, Euchel, and others), after which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. τῶν υἱῶν τοῦ μεταβάλλειν (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, those who must exchange this life for another), but such as are on the brink of the abyss. צדק in שׁפט־צדק is not equivalent to בּצדק, but is the accus. of the object, as at Zec 8:16, decide justice, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, so that justice is the result of thy judicial act; cf. Knobel on Deu 1:16. ודּין is imper., do right to the miserable and the poor; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.54.3">Psa 54:3</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.22.16">Jer 22:16</reference>; Jer 5:28. That is a king of a right sort, who directs his high function as a judge, so as to be an advocate [<hi type="italic">procurator</hi>] for the helpless of his people.
entries.f1d3df9bd92af3141fb5baf7aae89948471d3ead: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.10">Pro 31:10</reference> <div eID="gen12010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12011" type="x-p"/> A wife, such as she ought to be, is a rare treasure, a good excelling all earthly possession: 10 א A virtuous woman, who findeth her!         She stands far above pearls in worth. <div eID="gen12011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12012" type="x-p"/> In the connection אושׁת חיל and the like, the idea of bodily vigour is spiritualized to that of capacity, ability, and is generalized; in virtus the corresponding transition from manliness, and in the originally Romanic “<hi type="italic">Bravheit</hi>,” valour to ability, is completed; we have translated as at <reference osisRef="Prov.12.4">Pro 12:4</reference>, but also Luther, “a virtuous woman,” is suitable, since <hi type="italic">Tugend</hi> (virtue) has with <hi type="italic">Tüchtigkeit</hi> [ability] the same root-word, and according to our linguistic [German] usage designates the property of moral goodness and propriety, while for those of former times, when they spoke of the <hi type="italic">tugend</hi> (<hi type="italic">tugent</hi>) of a woman, the word combined with it the idea of fine manners (cf. חן, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.16">Pro 11:16</reference>) and culture (cf. שׂכל טוב, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.15">Pro 13:15</reference>). The question מי ימצא, <hi type="italic">quis inveniat</hi>, which, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.24">Ecc 7:24</reference>, proceeds from the supposition of the impossibility of finding, conveys here only the idea of the difficulty of finding. In ancient Jerusalem, when one was married, they were wont to ask: מצא אומוצא, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, has he found? thus as is said at <reference osisRef="Prov.18.22">Pro 18:22</reference>, or at Ecc 7:26. A virtuous woman [<hi type="italic">braves Weib</hi>] is not found by every one, she is found by comparatively few. In 10b there is given to the thought which underlies the question a synonymous expression. Ewald, Elster, and Zöckler incorrectly render the ו by “although” or “and yet.” Fleischer rightly: the second clause, if not in form yet in sense, runs parallel to the first. מכר designates the price for which such a woman is sold, and thus is purchasable, not without reference to this, that in the Orient a wife is obtained by means of מהר. מכר, synon. מחיר, for which a wife of the right kind is gained, is רחוק, placed further, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, is more difficult to be obtained, than pearls (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding “pearls” at <reference osisRef="Prov.3.15">Pro 3:15</reference>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, than the price for such precious things. The poet thereby means to say that such a wife is a more precious possession than all earthly things which are precious, and that he who finds such an one has to speak of his rare fortune.
entries.b6ef83f7a2867594d047cec5522421d5994092e8: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.11">Pro 31:11</reference> <div eID="gen12012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12013" type="x-p"/> The reason for this is now given: 11 ב The heart of her husband doth trust her,         And he shall not fail of grain. <div eID="gen12013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12014" type="x-p"/> If we interpret שׁלל, after <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.8">Ecc 9:8</reference>, as subject, then we miss לּו; it will thus be object., and the husband subj. to לא יחסּר: <hi type="italic">nec lucro carebit</hi>, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Fleischer translates it, with the remark that שׁלל denotes properly the spoil which one takes from an enemy, but then also, like the Arab. ḍanymat, can mean profit and gain of all kinds (cf. Rödiger in Gesenius’ <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>.). Thus also in our “<hi type="italic">kriegen</hi>” = to come into possession, the reference to war disappears. Hitzig understands by שׁלל, the continual prosperity of the man on account of his fortunate possession of such a wife; but in that case the poet should have said שׂמחת שׁלל; for שׁלל is gain, not the feeling that is therewith connected. There is here meant the gain, profit, which the housewife is the means of bringing in (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.78.13">Psa 78:13</reference>). The heart of her husband (בּעלּהּ) can be at rest, it can rest on her whom it loves - he goes after his calling, perhaps a calling which, though weighty and honourable, brings in little or nothing; but the wife keeps the family possessions scrupulously together, and increases them by her laborious and prudent management, so that there is not wanting to him gain, which he properly did not acquire, but which the confidence he is justified in reposing in his wife alone brings to him. She is to him a perpetual spring of nothing but good.
entries.8b12fbd927eb6d179a6c016ac7611333459e15d2: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.12">Pro 31:12</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.12">12</reference> ג She doeth good to him, and not evil,        All the days of her life; or, as Luther translates: <div eID="gen12014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12015" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Sie thut jm liebs und kein leids</hi>.” [She does him good, and no harm.] <div eID="gen12015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12016" type="x-p"/> She is far from ever doing him evil, she does him only good all her life long; her love is not dependent on freaks, it rests on deep moral grounds, and hence derives its power and purity, which remain ever the same. גּמל signifies to accomplish, to perform. To the not assimilated form גּמלתהוּ, cf. יסּרתּוּ, 1b.
entries.0cde3e45d7a5dbe2147cbff717db98049f6bdae7: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.13">Pro 31:13</reference> <div eID="gen12016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12017" type="x-p"/> The poet now describes how she disposes of things: 13 ד She careth for wool and flax,         And worketh these with her hands’ pleasure. <div eID="gen12017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12018" type="x-p"/> The verb דּרשׁ proceeds, as the Arab. shows,<note placement="foot">The inquirer is there called (Arab.) daras, as <hi type="italic">libros terens</hi>.</note> from the primary meaning <hi type="italic">terere</hi>; but to translate with reference thereto: <hi type="italic">tractat lanam et linum</hi> (lxx, Schultens, Dathe, Rosemüller, Fleischer), is inadmissible. The Heb. דרשׁ does not mean the external working at or manufacturing of a thing; but it means, even when it refers to this, the intention of the mind purposely directed thereto. Thus wool and flax come into view as the material of work which she cares to bring in; and ותּעשׂ signifies the work itself, following the creation of the need of work. Hitzig translates the second line: she works at the business of her hands. Certainly ב after עשׂה may denote the sphere of activity, <reference osisRef="Exod.31.4">Exo 31:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.31.1">1</reference> Kings 5:30, etc.; but if חפץ had here the weakened signification business, πρᾶγμα, - which it gains in the same way as we say business, affair, of any object of care - the scarcely established meaning presents itself, that she shows herself active in that which she has made the business of her hands. How much more beautiful, on the contrary, is the thought: she is active with her hands’ pleasure! חפץ is, as Schultens rightly explains, <hi type="italic">inclinatio flexa et propensa in aliquid</hi>, and <hi type="italic">pulchre manibus diligentissimis attribuitur lubentia cum oblectatione et per oblectationem sese animans</hi>. עשׂה, without obj. accus., signifies often: to accomplish, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Ps. 22:32; here it stands, in a sense, complete in itself, and without object. accus., as when it means “<hi type="italic">handeln</hi>” [<hi type="italic">agere</hi>], <reference osisRef="Prov.13.16">Pro 13:16</reference>, and particularly to act in the service of God = to offer sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Exod.10.25">Exo 10:25</reference>; it means here, and at Rth 2:19; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Hab 2:4</reference>, to be active, as at <reference osisRef="Isa.19.15">Isa 19:15</reference>, to be effective; ותּעשׂ is equivalent to ותעשׂ בּמּלאכה or ותעשׂ מלאכתּהּ (cf. under <reference osisRef="Prov.10.4">Pro 10:4</reference>). And pleasure and love for the work, חפץ, can be attributed to the hands with the same right as at <reference osisRef="Ps.78.72">Psa 78:72</reference>, discretion. The disposition which animates a man, especially his inner relation to the work devolving upon him, communicates itself to his hands, which, according as he has joy or aversion in regard to his work, will be nimble or clumsy. The Syr. translates: “and her hands are active after the pleasure of her heart;” but בחפץ is not equivalent to כּחפצהּ; also בּחפץ, in the sense of <hi type="italic">con amore</hi> (Böttcher), is not used.
entries.0ec0545d509686addaa90cba5628951720a96527: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.14">Pro 31:14</reference> <div eID="gen12018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12019" type="x-p"/> The following proverb praises the extent of her housewifely transactions: 14 ה She is like the ships of the merchant -         Bringeth her food from afar. <div eID="gen12019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12020" type="x-p"/> She is (lxx ἐγένετο) like merchant ships (כּאניות, indeterminate, and thus to be read kōǒnı̂joth), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, she has the art of such ships as sail away and bring wares from a distance, are equipped, sent out, and managed by an enterprising spirit; so the prudent, calculating look of the brave wife, directed towards the care and the advancement of her house, goes out beyond the nearest circle; she descries also distant opportunities of advantageous purchase and profitable exchange, and brings in from a distance what is necessary for the supply of her house, or, mediately, what yields this supply (ממּרחק, Cod. <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>. ממרחק, cf. under <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Isa 10:6</reference>), for she finds that source of gain she has espied.
entries.b43cd9b8d2f9f1d62fd250936402fc2348a1e9f3: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.15">Pro 31:15</reference> <div eID="gen12020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12021" type="x-p"/> With this diligence in her duties she is not a long sleeper, who is not awakened till the sun is up; but 15 ו She riseth up while it is yet night,        And giveth food to her house,        And the fixed portion to her maidens. <div eID="gen12021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12022" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. express, if not a logical sequence of connection, yet a close inner binding together of the separate features of the character here described. Early, ere the morning dawns, such a housewife rises up, because she places care for her house above her own comfort; or rather, because this care is to her a satisfaction and a joy. Since now the poet means without doubt to say that she is up before the other inmates of the house, especially before the children, though not before the maids: we have not, in ותּתּן, to think that the inmates of the house, all in the morning night-watch, stand round about her, and that each receives from her a portion for the approaching day; but that she herself, early, whilst yet the most are asleep, gives out or prepares the necessary portions of food for the day (cf. ויּתּן, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Isa 53:9</reference>). Regarding טרף, food, from טרף (to tear in pieces, viz., with the teeth), and regarding חק, a portion decreed, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 30:8. It is true that חק also means the appointed labour (<hi type="italic">pensum</hi>), and thus the day’s work (דּבר יום); but the parallelism brings it nearer to explain after <reference osisRef="Prov.30.8">Pro 30:8</reference>, as is done by Gesenius and Hitzig after Exo 5:14.
entries.fe1f901bfa5543997d409a9804b37923235f9f66: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.16">Pro 31:16</reference> <div eID="gen12022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12023" type="x-p"/> This industry - a pattern for the whole house - this punctuality in the management of household matters, secures to her success in the extension of her household wealth: 16 ז She seeketh a field and getteth possession of it;        Of the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard. <div eID="gen12023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12024" type="x-p"/> The field which she considereth, towards which her wish and her effort are directed, is perhaps not one beyond those which she already possesses, but one which has hitherto been wanting to her family; for the poet has, after <reference osisRef="Prov.31.23">Pro 31:23</reference>, an inhabitant of a town in his eye, - a woman whose husband is not a landlord, but has a business in the city. The perf. זממה precedes and gives circumstantiality to the chief <hi type="italic">factum</hi> expressed by ותּקּחה. Regarding זמם, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 21:27. “לקח is the general expression for purchasing, as נתן, 24b, for selling. Thus the Aram. and Arab. אחד, while, (Arab.) akhadh w'ṭa, Turk. alisch werisch (from elmeḳ, to take, and wirmek, to give - viz. ṣâtun, in the way of selling; Lat. <hi type="italic">venum</hi>), post-bibl. משּׂא וּמתּן or מקּח וּממכּר, denotes giving and taking = business in general” (Fleischer). In 16b the Chethı̂b is, with Ewald and Bertheau, to be read נטע, and, with Hitzig, to be made dependent on ותקחה, as parallel obj.: “of her hands’ fruit (she gaineth) a planting of vines.” But a planting of vines would be expressed by מטּע כרם (Mic 1:6); and the Kerı̂ נטעה is more acceptable. The perf., as a fundamental verbal form, is here the expression of the abstract present: she plants a vineyard, for she purchases vines from the profit of her industry (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.23">Isa 7:23</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.5.2">Pro 5:2</reference>).
entries.38c37cde4d84c521b59e4d86e7421c86045797cd: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.17">Pro 31:17</reference> <div eID="gen12024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12025" type="x-p"/> The poet has this augmented household wealth in his eye, for he continues: 17 ח She girdeth her loins with strength,         And moveth vigorously her arms. <div eID="gen12025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12026" type="x-p"/> Strength is as the girdle which she wraps around her body (<reference osisRef="Ps.93.1">Psa 93:1</reference>). We write חגרה בעוז; both words have <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, and the ב of בעוז is aspirated. Thus girded with strength, out of this fulness of strength she makes firm or steels her arms (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.89.22">Psa 89:22</reference>). The produce of the field and vineyard extend far beyond the necessity of her house; thus a great portion is brought to sale, and the gain thence arising stimulates the industry and the diligence of the unwearied woman.
entries.138f03fe3187a5228c9fda7d3fee748eb4e2f04e: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.18">Pro 31:18</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.18">18</reference> ט She perceiveth that her gain is good;         And her light goeth not out at night. <div eID="gen12026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12027" type="x-p"/> The perf. and fut. are related to each other as antecedent and consequent, so that 18a can also be rendered as an hypothetical antecedent. She comes to find (taste) how profitable her industry is by the experience resulting from the sale of its product: the corn, the grapes, and the wine are found to be good, and thus her gain (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.3.14">Pro 3:14</reference>) is better, this opened new source of nourishment productive. <div eID="gen12027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12028" type="x-p"/> This spurs on her active industry to redoubled effort, and at times, when she is not fully occupied by the oversight of her fields and vineyard, she has another employment over which her light goes not out till far in the night. בּלּילה is, as at <reference osisRef="Lam.2.19">Lam 2:19</reference>, a needless Kerı̂ for the poetic בּלּיל (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.3">Isa 16:3</reference>). What other business it is to which she gives attention till in the night, is mentioned in the next verse.
entries.c07e6222a53bffab6a62d75d328d7af194426a37: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.19">Pro 31:19</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.19">19</reference> י She putteth her hand to the rock Spinnrocken;        And her fingers lay hold on the spindle. <div eID="gen12028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12029" type="x-p"/> She applies herself to the work of spinning, and performs it with skill. The phrase שׁלּח יד בּ (שׁלח, <reference osisRef="Job.28.9">Job 28:9</reference>) signifies to take up an object of work, and תּמך, with obj. accus. (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.1.5">Amo 1:5</reference>), the handling of the instrument of work necessary thereto. כּפּים denotes the hands when the subject is skilful, successful work; we accordingly say יגיע כפים, not יגיע ידים; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.31.13">Pro 31:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.31.16">Pro 31:16</reference>, Psa 78:72. What פּלך means is shown by the Arab. falakat, which, as distinguished from mighzal, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, <hi type="italic">fuseau</hi> (Lat. <hi type="italic">fusus</hi>), is explained by <hi type="italic">bout arrondi et conique au bas du fuseau</hi>, thus: the whorl, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the ring or knob fastened on the spindle below, which gives it its necessary weight and regulates its movement, Lat. <hi type="italic">verticellus</hi>, post-bibl. פּיקה (which Bartenora glosses by the Ital. <hi type="italic">fusajuolo</hi>) or צנּורה, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">Kelim</hi> ix. 6, כושׁ שׁבלע את הצנורה, a spindle which holds the whorl hidden (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Aruch under כש, iii.). But the word then also signifies <hi type="italic">per synecd</hi>o<hi type="italic">chen partis pro toto</hi>, the spindle, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the cylindrical wood on which the thread winds itself when spinning (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.29">2Sa 3:29</reference>, where it means the staff on which the infirm leans); Homer gives to Helen and the goddesses golden spindles (χρυσηλάκατοι). Accordingly it is not probable that כּישׁור also denotes the whorl, as Kimchi explains the word: “כישור is that which one calls by the name <hi type="italic">verteil</hi>, viz., that which one fixes on the spindle (פלך) above to regulate the spinning (מטוה),” according to which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. renders כישׁור by σφόνδυλος, whorl, and פלך by ἄτρακτος, spindle. The old interpreters have not recognised that כישׁור denotes a thing belonging to the spinning apparatus; the lxx, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, Syr., and Jerome see therein an ethical idea (from כּשׁר, to be capable, able); but Luther, not misled thereby, translates with unusual excellence: <div eID="gen12029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12030" type="x-p"/> She stretches her hand to the rock, <div eID="gen12030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12031" type="x-p"/> And her fingers grasp the spindle. <div eID="gen12031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12032" type="x-p"/> He has in this no predecessors, except only the Targumists, whose כוּנשׁרא (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Levy) appears also to denote the spinning-rock. The Syriac and Talmudic כּוּשׁ, which is compared by Gesenius-Dietrich, is another word, and denotes, not the rock, but the spindle. Immanuel also, who explains פלך as the מעזל, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the spindle, understands (as perhaps also Parchon) by כישׁור the rock. And why should not the rock (<hi type="italic">wocken</hi> = distaff), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the stock to which the tuft of flax, hemp, or wool is fixed for the purpose of being spun, Lat. <hi type="italic">colus</hi>, not be named כּישׁור, from כשׁר, to be upright as a stick, upright in height, or perhaps more correctly as מכשׁיר, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as that which prepares or makes fit the flax for spinning? Also in צינק, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.26">Jer 29:26</reference>, there are united the meanings of the close and the confining dungeon, and שׁלה = שׁילון signifies<note placement="foot">Otherwise, but improbably, Schultens: <hi type="italic">colus a</hi> כשׁר = katr kathr, <hi type="italic">necti in orbem, circumnecti in globum</hi>. In פּלך, whence פּלך, he rightly finds the primary meaning of <hi type="italic">circumvolutio sive gyratio</hi>.</note> the place which yields rest. The spinning-wheel is a German invention of the 16th century, but the rock standing on the ground, or held also in the hands, the spindle and the whorl, are more ancient.<note placement="foot">A view of the ancient art of spinning is afforded by the figures of the 12th Dynasty (according to Lepsius, 2380-2167 b.c.) in the burial chamber of <hi type="italic">Beni Hassan</hi> (270 kilometres above Bulak, on the right bank of the Nile). M. J. Henry, in his work <hi type="italic">L'Egypte Pharaonique</hi> (Paris 1846), Bd. 2, p. 431, mentions that there are figures there which represent “<hi type="italic">toutes les opérations de la fabrication des tissus depuis le filage jusqu au tissage</hi>.” Then he continues: <hi type="italic">Lex fuseaux dont se servent les fileuses sont excatement semblables aux nôtres, et on voit même ces fileuses imprimer le mouvement de rotation à ces fuseaux, en en froissant le bout inferieur entre leur main et leur cuisse</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen12032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12033" type="x-p"/> With the spindle תמך stands in fit relation, for it is twirled between the fingers, as Catullus says of Fate:<hi type="italic">Libratum tereti versabat pollice fusum</hi>.<note placement="foot">In the “marriage of Peleus and Thetis,” Catullus describes the work of the Fates: “Their hands are ceaselessly active at their never-ending work; while the left holds the rock, surrounded with a soft fleece, the right assiduously draws the thread and forms it with raised fingers; then it swiftly turns the spindle, with the thumb stretched down, and swings it away in whirling circles.” Then follows the refrain of the song of the Fates: <hi type="italic">Currite ducentes subtegmina, currite, fusi</hi>. - (After Hertzberg’s Translation.)</note>
entries.13386685e29651078ed6c8427d51aaa82b8f8d95: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.20">Pro 31:20</reference> <div eID="gen12033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12034" type="x-p"/> That which impels the housewife to this labour is not selfishness, not a narrow-hearted limitation of her care to the circle of what is her own, but love, which reaches out far beyond this circle: 20 כ She holdeth out her hand to the unfortunate,         And stretcheth forth her hands to the needy. <div eID="gen12034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12035" type="x-p"/> With כּפּיה, 19b, is connected the idea of artistic skilfulness; with כּפּהּ, here that of offering for counsel (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Isa.2.6">Isa 2:6</reference>); with sympathy and readiness to help, she presents herself to those who are oppressed by the misfortunes of life as if for an alliance, as if saying: place confidence in me, I shall do whatever I can - there thou hast my hand! Hitzig erroneously thinks of the open hand with a gift lying in it: this ought to be named, for כף in itself is nothing else than the half-opened hand. Also in 20b we are not to think of alms. Here Hitzig rightly: she stretches out to him both of her hands, that he might grasp them, both of them, or whichever he may. She does not throw to him merely a gift from a distance, but above all she gives to him to experience her warm sympathy (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.49">Eze 16:49</reference>). Here, as at 19a, שׁלחה is punctuated (with <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>) as <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>. The punctuation supposes that the author both times not unintentionally made use of the intensive form. This one verse (20) is complete in itself as a description of character; and the author has done well in choosing such strong expressions, for, without this sympathy with misery and poverty, she, so good and trustworthy and industrious, might indeed be pleasing to her husband, but not to God. One could almost wish that greater expansion had been given to this one feature in the picture.
entries.8a1b77518609947a91eb792890911b7a68b17cd1: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.21">Pro 31:21</reference> <div eID="gen12035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12036" type="x-p"/> But the poet goes on to describe her fruitful activity in the nearest sphere of her calling: 21 ל She is not afraid of the snow for her house;         For her whole house is clothed in scarlet. <div eID="gen12036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12037" type="x-p"/> A fall of snow in the rainy season of winter is not rare in Palestine, the Hauran, and neighbouring countries, and is sometimes accompanied with freezing cold.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., regarding a fall of snow in Jerusalem, the journal <hi type="italic">Saat auf Hoffnung Jahrg</hi>. 3, Heft 3; and in the Hauran Comm. to Job 38:22.</note> <div eID="gen12037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12038" type="x-p"/> She sees approaching the cold time of the year without any fear for her house, even though the season bring intense cold; for her whole house, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the whole of the members of her family, are לבשׁ שׁנים. The connection is accusatival (<hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ἐνδεδυμένος ἐρυθρά), as at <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.32">2Sa 15:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.2">Eze 9:2</reference>-3. שׁני, from שׁנה, to shine, glance clear, or high red, and is with or without תולעת the name of the colour of the <hi type="italic">Kermes</hi> worm, crimson or scarlet, perhaps to be distinguished from ארגּמן, the red-purple shell colour, and תּכלת, the blue. שׁנים are clothing or material coloured with such שׁני (bright red) (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Isa 1:18</reference>). The explanation of the word by <hi type="italic">dibapha</hi> is inadmissible, because the doubled colouring, wherever it is mentioned, always refers to the purple, particularly that of Tyre (<hi type="italic">dibapha Tyria</hi>), not to the scarlet.<note placement="foot">Vid., Blümner’s <hi type="italic">Die gewerbliche Thâtigkeit der Völder des klassischen Alterthums</hi> (1869), p. 21f.</note> <div eID="gen12038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12039" type="x-p"/> But why does the poet name scarlet-coloured clothing? On account of the contrast to the white snow, says Hitzig, he clothes the family in crimson. But this contrast would be a meaningless freak. Rather it is to be supposed that there is ascribed to the red material a power of retaining the heat, as there is to the white that of keeping off the heat; but evidence for this are wanting. Therefore Rosenmüller, Vaihinger, and Böttcher approve of the translation <hi type="italic">duplicibus</hi> (Jerome, Luther) [= with double clothing], because they read, with the lxx, שׁנים.<note placement="foot">The lxx reads together שנים מרבדים, δισσὰς χλαίνας, and brings into <reference osisRef="Prov.31.21">Pro 31:21</reference> (her husband remains without care for the members of the family if it does not snow χιονίζη, as it is to be read for χρονίζη) and 22 the husband, who appears to the translator too much kept in the background.</note> <div eID="gen12039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12040" type="x-p"/> But, with right, the Syr., Targ. abide by זהוריתא, scarlet. The scarlet clothing is of wool, which as such preserves warmth, and, as high-coloured, appears at the same time dignified (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.24">2Sa 1:24</reference>).
entries.4f3acf8f54420780d366aea467c6097da317dd74: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.22">Pro 31:22</reference> <div eID="gen12040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12041" type="x-p"/> From the protecting, and at the same time ornamental clothing of the family, the poet proceeds to speak of the bed-places, and of the attire of the housewife: 22 מ She prepareth for herself pillows;         Linen and purple is her raiment. <div eID="gen12041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12042" type="x-p"/> Regarding מרבדּים (with ב <hi type="italic">raphatum</hi>), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 7:16. Thus, pillows or mattresses (Aquila, Theodotion, περιστρώματα; Jerome, <hi type="italic">stragulatam vestem</hi>; Luther, <hi type="italic">Decke</hi> = coverlets) to make the bed soft and to adorn it (Kimchi: ליפּות על המטות, according to which <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. κόσμια); Symmachus designates it as ἀμφιτάπους, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, τάπητες (<hi type="italic">tapetae, tapetia</hi>, carpets), which are hairy (shaggy) on both sides.<note placement="foot">Vid., Lumbroso, <hi type="italic">Recherches sur l'Economie politique de l'Egypte sous les Lagides</hi> (Turin, 1870), p. 111; <hi type="italic">des tapis de laine de premeère qualité, pourpres, laineux des deux côtés</hi> (ἀμφίταποι).</note> <div eID="gen12042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12043" type="x-p"/> Only the lxx makes out of it δισσὰς χλαίνας, lined overcoats, for it brings over שׁנים. By עשׂתה־לּהּ it is not meant that she prepares such pillows for her own bed, but that she herself (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, for the wants of her house) prepares them. But she also clothes herself in costly attire. שׁשׁ (an Egyptian word, not, as Heb., derived from שׁוּשׁ, cogn. ישׁשׁ, to be white) is the old name for linen, according to which the Aram. translates it by בּוּץ, the Greek by βύσσος, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, pp. 470, 557, to which the remark is to be added, that the linen [Byssus], according to a prevailing probability, was not a fine cotton cloth, but linen cloth. Luther translates שׁשׁ, here and elsewhere, by <hi type="italic">weisse Seide</hi> [white silk] (σηρικόν, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, from the land of the Σῆρες, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.12">Rev 18:12</reference>); but the silk, is first mentioned by Ezekiel under the name of משׁי; and the ancients call the country where silk-stuff (<hi type="italic">bombycina</hi>) was woven, uniformly Assyria. ארגּמן (Aram. ארגּון, derived by Benfey, with great improbability, from the rare Sanscrit word râgavant, red-coloured; much rather from רגם = רקם, as stuff of variegated colour) is red purple; the most valuable purple garments were brought from Tyre and Sidon.
entries.06897d6ab43f1b3673202914029fff731eebd189: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.23">Pro 31:23</reference> <div eID="gen12043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12044" type="x-p"/> Now, first, the description turns back to the husband, of the woman who is commended, mentioned in the introduction: 23 נ 32 Well known in the gates is her husband,        Where he sitteth among the elders of the land. <div eID="gen12044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12045" type="x-p"/> Such a wife is, according to <reference osisRef="Prov.12.4">Pro 12:4</reference>, עטרת בּעלּהּ, - she advances the estimation and the respect in which her husband is held. He has, in the gates where the affairs of the city are deliberated upon, a well-known, reputable name; for there he sits, along with the elders of the land, who are chosen into the council of the city as the chief place of the land, and has a weighty voice among them. The phrase wavers between נודע (lxx περίβλεπτος γίνεται; <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ἔλνωσται) and נודע. The old Venetian edd. have in this place (like the Cod. <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>.), and at <reference osisRef="Ps.9.17">Psa 9:17</reference>, נודע; on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.2">Psa 76:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.10">Ecc 6:10</reference>, נודע, and that is correct; for the Masora, at this place and at <reference osisRef="Ps.76.2">Psa 76:2</reference> (in the <hi type="italic">Biblia rabb</hi>), is disfigured.
entries.0ee64941457c2f1793b9c6eb28bbf162e41b6709: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.24">Pro 31:24</reference> <div eID="gen12045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12046" type="x-p"/> The description, following the order of the letters, now directs attention to the profitable labour of the housewife: 24 ס She prepareth body-linen and selleth it,         And girdles doth she give to the Phoenicians. <div eID="gen12046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12047" type="x-p"/> It is a question whether סדין signifies σινδών, cloth from <hi type="italic">Sindhu</hi>, the land of India (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Isa.3.23">Isa 3:23</reference>); the Arab. sadn (sadl), to cause to hang down, to descend (for the purpose of covering or veiling), offers an appropriate verbal root. In the Talmud, סדין is the sleeping linen, the curtain, the embroidered cloth, but particularly a light smock-frock, as summer costume, which was worn on the bare body (cf. Mar 14:51.). Kimchi explains the word by night-shirt; the <hi type="italic">Edictum Diocletiani</hi>, xviii. 16, names σινδόνες κοιταρίαι, as the <hi type="italic">Papyrus Louvre</hi>, ὀθόνια ἐγκοιμήτρια; and the connection in the Edict shows that linen attire (ἐκ λίνου) is meant, although - as with שׁשׁ, so also with סדין - with the ancients and the moderns, sometimes linen and sometimes cotton is spoken of without any distinction. Aethicus speaks of costly girdles, <hi type="italic">Cosmogr</hi>. 84, as fabricated at Jerusalem: <hi type="italic">baltea regalia ... ex Hierosolyma allata</hi>; Jerusalem and Scythopolis were in later times the chief places in Palestine for the art of weaving. In Galilee also, where excellent flax grew, the art of weaving was carried on; and the ὀθόναι, which, according to Clemens Alex. <hi type="italic">Paedag</hi>. ii. 10, p. 239, were exported ἐκ γῆς Ἑβραίων, are at least in their material certainly synon. with σινδόνες. Regarding נתן, syn. מכר, opp. לקח, syn. נשׂא = קנה, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at 16a. There is no reason to interpret כּנעני here, with the obliteration of the ethnographical meaning, in the general sense of סחר, trader, merchant; for purple, 22b, is a Phoenician manufacture, and thus, as an article of exchange, can be transferred to the possession of the industrious wife.
entries.3ea2ca8850dcc3b66f53e11a2df01cc21c23c172: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.25">Pro 31:25</reference> <div eID="gen12047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12048" type="x-p"/> The description is now more inward: 25 ע Strength and honour is her clothing;         Thus she laugheth at the future day. <div eID="gen12048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12049" type="x-p"/> She is clothed with עז, strength, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, power over the changes of temporal circumstances, which easily shatter and bring to ruin a household resting on less solid foundations; clothed with הדר, glory, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, elevation above that which is low, little, common, a state in which they remain who propose to themselves no high aim after which they strive with all their might: in other words, her raiment is just pride, true dignity, with which she looks confidently into the future, and is armed against all sorrow and care. The connection of ideas, עז והדר (defectively written, on the contrary, at <reference osisRef="Ps.84.6">Psa 84:6</reference>, Masora, and only there written <hi type="italic">plene</hi>, and with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>), instead of the frequent הוד והדר, occurs only here. The expression 25b is like <reference osisRef="Job.39.7">Job 39:7</reference>, wherefore Hitzig rightly compares <reference osisRef="Job.24.14">Job 24:14</reference> to 25a. יום אחרון, distinguished from אחרית, and incorrectly interpreted (Rashi) of the day of death, is, as at <reference osisRef="Isa.30.8">Isa 30:8</reference>, the future, here that which one at a later period may enter upon.
entries.61c3c440225301b3b122ccd086587221e448225e: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.26">Pro 31:26</reference> <div eID="gen12049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12050" type="x-p"/> The next verse presents one of the most beautiful features in the portrait: 26 פ She openeth her mouth with wisdom,         And amiable instruction is on her tongue. <div eID="gen12050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12051" type="x-p"/> The ב of בּחכמה is, as also at <reference osisRef="Ps.49.5">Psa 49:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.2">Psa 78:2</reference>, that of means: when she speaks, then it is wisdom pressing itself from her heart outward, by means of which she breaks the silence of her mouth. With על, in the expression 26b, elsewhere תּהת interchanges: under the tongue, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.7">Psa 10:7</reference>, one has that which is ready to be spoken out, and on the tongue, <reference osisRef="Ps.15.3">Psa 15:3</reference>, that which is in the act of being spoken out. תּורת־חסד is a genitive connection after the manner of tôrath אמת, Mal 2:6. The gen. is not, as at <reference osisRef="Lev.6.2">Lev 6:2</reference>, in tôrath העלה, the gen. of the object (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Fleischer’s <hi type="italic">institutio ad humanitatem</hi>), but the gen. of property, but not so that חסד denotes grace (Symmachus, νόμος ἐπίχαρις; Theodotion, νόμος χάριτος), because for this meaning there is no example except <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6">Isa 40:6</reference>; and since חסד in the O.T. is the very same as in the N.T., love, which is the fulfilling of the law, Hos 6:6, cf. 1Ki 20:31,<note placement="foot">Immanuel remarks that Tôrath חסד probably refers to the Tôra, and שׁכוהל חסד, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, which is wholly love, which goes forth in love, to the <hi type="italic">Gesetz</hi> = statute.</note> it is supposed that the poet, since he writes תורת חסד, and not תורת חן, means to designate by חסד this property without which her love for her husband, her industry, her high sentiment, would be no virtues, viz., unselfish, sympathizing, gentle love. Instruction which bears on itself the stamp of such amiability, and is also gracious, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, awakening love, because going forth from love (according to which Luther, translating <hi type="italic">holdselige Lere</hi> = pleasing instructions, thus understands it) - such instruction she carries, as house-mother (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.8">Pro 1:8</reference>), in her mouth. Accordingly the lxx translate (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Lagarde regarding the mistakes of this text before us) θεσμοὶ ἐλεημοσύνης, and Jerome <hi type="italic">lex clementiae</hi>. חסד is related to אהבה as grace to love; it denotes love showing itself in kindness and gracefulness, particularly condescending love, proceeding from a compassionate sympathy with the sufferings and wants of men. Such graceful instruction she communicates now to this and now to that member of her household, for nothing that goes on in her house escapes her observation.
entries.5e298a54a5a6ebb5541216327314873a67cf71ad: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.27">Pro 31:27</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.27">27</reference> צ She looketh well to the ways of her house,         And eateth not the bread of idleness. <div eID="gen12051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12052" type="x-p"/> Although there exists an inner relation between 27a and <reference osisRef="Prov.31.26">Pro 31:26</reference>, yet 27a is scarcely to be thought of (Hitzig) as appos. to the suffix in לשׁונהּ. Participles with or without determination occur in descriptions frequently as predicates of the subject standing in the discourse of the same force as abstr. present declarations, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Isa 40:22., Psa 104:13. צופיּה is connected with the accus. of the object of the intended warning, like <reference osisRef="Prov.15.3">Pro 15:3</reference>, and is compared according to the form with המיּה, Pro 7:11. הליבה signifies elsewhere things necessary for a journey, <reference osisRef="Job.6.19">Job 6:19</reference>, and in the <hi type="italic">plur. magnificus</hi> it denotes show (<hi type="italic">pompa</hi>), <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Hab 3:6</reference> : but originally the walk, conduct, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.6">Nah 2:6</reference>; and here in the plur. walks = comings and goings, but not these separately, but in general, the <hi type="italic">modi procedendi</hi> (lxx διατριβαι). The Chethı̂b has הילכות, probably an error in writing, but possibly also the plur. of הלכה, thus found in the post-bibl. Heb. (after the form צדקות), custom, viz., appointed traditional law, but also like the Aram. הלכא (<hi type="italic">emph</hi>. הלכתא), usage, manner, common practice. Hitzig estimates this Chethı̂b, understood Talmudically, as removing the section into a late period; but this Talmudical signification is not at all appropriate (Hitzig translates, with an incorrect rendering of צופיה, “for she sees after the ordering of the house”), and besides the Aram. הלכא, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Targ. <reference osisRef="Prov.16.9">Pro 16:9</reference>, in the first line, signifies only the walk or the manner and way of going, and this gives with the Kerı̂ essentially the same signification. Luther well: <hi type="italic">Sie schawet wie es in jrem Hause zugeht</hi> [= she looks how it goes in her house]. Her eyes are turned everywhere; she is at one time here, at another there, to look after all with her own eyes; she does not suffer the day’s work, according to the instructions given, to be left undone, while she folds her own hands on her bosom; but she works, keeping an oversight on all sides, and does not eat the bread of idleness (עצלוּת = עצלה, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.15">Pro 19:15</reference>), but bread well deserved, for εἴ τις οὐ θέλει ἐργάζεσθαι, μηδὲ ἐσθιέτω, 2Th 3:10.
entries.826e6e8370a4e86971a086b75b0a008503aee58e: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.28">Pro 31:28</reference> <div eID="gen12052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12053" type="x-p"/> Now begins the finale of this song in praise of the virtuous woman: 28 ק Her sons rise up and bless her,         Her husband (riseth up) and praiseth her. <div eID="gen12053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12054" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> אשּׁר in such a connection is denom. of אשׁר (אשׁרי). Her children rise up (קוּם, like <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.17">Jer 26:17</reference>, but here, perhaps, with the associated idea of reverential honour) and bless her, that she has on her part brought the house and them to such prosperity, such a position of respect, and to a state where love (חסד) reigns, and her husband rises up and sings her praise.
entries.20c806101cd1ca5720c9fb89ab806f443461bf36: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.29">Pro 31:29</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.29">29</reference> ר “Many are the daughters who have done bravely,         But thou hast surpassed them all together.” <div eID="gen12054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12055" type="x-p"/> We have already often remarked, last time under <reference osisRef="Prov.29.6">Pro 29:6</reference>, that רב, not indeed in its sing., but in its plur. רבּים and רבּות, can precede, after the manner of a numeral, as attribute; but this syntactical licence, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.12">Pro 28:12</reference>, by no means appears, and needs to be assumed as little here as at <reference osisRef="Prov.8.26">Pro 8:26</reference>, although there is no reason that can be adduced against it. עשׂה חיל signifies here not the gaining of riches (the lxx, Syr., Targ., Jerome, Luther, Gesenius, Böttcher, and others), which here, where the encomium comes to its height, would give to it a mercenary mammon-worship note - it indeed has this signification only when connected with ל of the person: <hi type="italic">Sibi opes acquirere</hi>, <reference osisRef="Deut.6.17">Deu 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.4">Eze 28:4</reference> - but: bravery, energy, and, as the reference to אשׁת חיל demands, moral activity, capacity for activity, in accordance with one’s calling, ποιεῖν ἀρετήν, by which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates it. בּנות is, as in the primary passages, <reference osisRef="Gen.30.13">Gen 30:13</reference>; Sol 6:9, a more delicate, finer name of women than נשׁים: many daughters there have always been who have unfolded ability, but thou my spouse hast raised thyself above them all, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, thou art excellent and incomparable. Instead of עלית, there is to be written, after Chajug, Aben Ezra (<hi type="italic">Zachoth</hi> 7a), and Jekuthiel under <reference osisRef="Gen.16.11">Gen 16:11</reference>, עלית; the Spanish <hi type="italic">Nakdanim</hi> thus distinguish the forms מצאת, thou hast found, and מצאת, she has found. כּלּנה, for כּלּן, Gen 42:36.
entries.7f55a46599a8aeac93c90edbffc9f756c1ba1acd: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.30">Pro 31:30</reference> <div eID="gen12055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12056" type="x-p"/> What now follows is not a continuation of the husband’s words of praise (Ewald, Elster, Löwenstein), but an <hi type="italic">epiphonema auctoris</hi> (Schultens); the poet confirms the praise of the husband by referring it to the general ground of its reason: 30 ש Grace is deceit; and beauty, vanity -         A wife that feareth Jahve, she shall be praised. <div eID="gen12056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12057" type="x-p"/> Grace is deceit, because he who estimates the works of a wife merely by the loveliness of her external appearance, is deceived by it; and beauty is vanity, <hi type="italic">vanitas</hi>, because it is nothing that remains, nothing that is real, but is subject to the law of all material things - transitoriness. The true value of a wife is measured only by that which is enduring, according to the moral background of its external appearance; according to the piety which makes itself manifest when the beauty of bodily form has faded away, in a beauty which is attractive.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., the application of <reference osisRef="Prov.31.30">Pro 31:30</reference> in <hi type="italic">Taanith</hi> 26b: “Young man,” say the maidens, “lift up thine eyes and behold that which thou choosest for thyself! Direct thine eyes not to beauty (נוי), direct thine eyes to the family (משׁפחה); pleasantness is a deception, etc.”</note> יראת (with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> following),<note placement="foot">The writing יראת־ is that of Ben Asher, יראת that of Ben Naphtali; Norzi, from a misunderstanding, claims יראת־ (with <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi>) as Ben Asher’s manner of writing.</note> is here the connective form of יראה (fem. of ירא). The <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. תתהלּל is here manifestly (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.2">Pro 27:2</reference>) not reflexive, but representative of the passive (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.12.8">Pro 12:8</reference>, and the frequently occurring מהלּל, <hi type="italic">laudatus</hi> = <hi type="italic">laudandus</hi>), nowhere occurring except in the passage before us. In itself the fut. may also mean: she will be praised = is worthy of praise, but the jussive rendering (Luther: Let her be praised) is recommended by the verse which follows:
entries.ab5fd749d7f2b54153608852f69b71878feb8091: <reference osisRef="Prov.31.31">Pro 31:31</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.31">31</reference> ת Give to her of the fruit of her hands;         And let her works praise her in the gates! <div eID="gen12057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12058" type="x-p"/> The fruit of her hands is the good which, by her conduct, she has brought to maturity - the blessing which she has secured for others, but, according to the promise (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.10">Isa 3:10</reference>), has also secured for her own enjoyment. The first line proceeds on the idea that, on account of this blessing, she herself shall rejoice. תּנוּ־להּ (with <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi>, after <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>-<hi type="italic">Setzung</hi>, §37) is not equivalent to give to her honour because of...; for in that case, instead of the ambiguous מן, another preposition - such <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, as על - would have been used; and so תּנוּ, of itself, cannot be equivalent to תּנּוּ (sing the praise of), as Ziegler would read, after Jdg 11:40. It must stand with כבוד, or instead of מפּרי an accus. obj. is to be thought of, as at <reference osisRef="Ps.68.35">Psa 68:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.3">Deu 32:3</reference>, which the necessity of the case brings with it - the giving, as a return in the echo of the song of praise. Immanuel is right in explaining תנו־לה by תגמלו לה חסד or עשׂו עתה חסד וכבוד, cf. Psa 28:4. The מן, as is not otherwise to be expected, after תנו is partitive: give to her something of the fruit of her hands, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, recompense it to her, render it thankfully, by which not exclusively a requital in the form of honourable recognition, but yet this specially, is to be thought of. Her best praise is her works themselves. In the gates, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, in the place where the representatives of the people come together, and where the people are assembled, her works praise her; and the poet desires that this may be right worthily done, full of certainty that she merits it, and that they honour themselves who seek to praise the works of such a woman, which carry in themselves their own commendation.  <chapter eID="Prov.31"/> <div eID="gen12058" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen10356" osisID="Prov" type="book"/>

                  <ns0:p n="17">17 She girdeth her loins with strength <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">She useth great diligence and expedition in her employment; for which end men in those times use to gird up their long and loose garments about their loins.</ns0:note>, and strengtheneth her arms <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Putteth forth her utmost strength in her business.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="21">21 She is not afraid of the snow <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or of any injuries of the weather.</ns0:note> for her houshold: for all her houshold are cloathed with <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
